note: Authored offline and committed. The server only reads this file - it never generates items per request, because items that differ per learner cannot be compared across learners, calibrated from response data, or A/B tested, and their answer keys are never reviewed. Expand with `npm run author:quiz`, then review the keys before committing.
difficultyMeaning: An item of difficulty d is expected to be answerable by a learner at level >= d on the 0-5 scale.

items.stem: What does `[x * 2 for x in range(3)]` evaluate to?
items.rationale: range(3) yields 0, 1, 2, and each is doubled.

items.stem: A function is defined as `def add(item, acc=[])`. What happens across repeated calls that omit `acc`?

options.text: A fresh empty list is created on each call
Every such call shares the same list object
Python raises a TypeError for mutable defaults
The default is silently converted to a tuple

items.rationale: Default arguments are evaluated once, at definition time, so the list persists between calls.

items.stem: Which clause filters rows after GROUP BY has aggregated them?

options.text: WHERE
ORDER BY
HAVING
DISTINCT

items.rationale: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters the aggregated groups.

items.stem: You write a LEFT JOIN, then add `WHERE right_table.status = 'active'`. What happens?

options.text: All left rows are kept, with the condition ignored for NULLs
The query fails to parse
It is identical to putting the condition in the ON clause
Unmatched left rows are dropped, so it behaves like an inner join

items.rationale: Unmatched rows have NULL on the right, and NULL = 'active' is not true, so WHERE removes them. Putting the condition in ON would preserve them.

items.stem: What does a 95% confidence interval actually claim?

options.text: If the procedure were repeated on many samples, 95% of the intervals produced would contain the true value
There is a 95% probability the true value lies inside this particular interval
95% of the observed data points fall inside the interval
The estimate is accurate to within 5%

items.rationale: The 95% is a property of the procedure across repeated samples, not of the one interval you computed.

items.stem: A test returns p = 0.03. What does that number mean?

options.text: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
If the null hypothesis were true, data at least this extreme would occur 3% of the time
There is a 97% chance the effect is real
The effect size is 3%

items.rationale: A p-value is computed assuming the null is true; it says nothing directly about the probability of any hypothesis.

items.stem: You left-join a table on `id`, and the right table has two rows with the same `id`. What happens to that left row?

options.text: The output always has exactly as many rows as the left table
The join raises an error on duplicate keys
It is duplicated - one output row per match
Only the first match is kept

items.rationale: A join is a filtered cross product per key, so duplicate keys on the right multiply left rows. Checking row counts after a join catches this.

items.stem: In pandas, `df[df.score > 10].flag = 1` usually leaves `df` unchanged. Why?

options.text: Boolean masks return immutable views
Columns cannot be assigned to after filtering
It does modify df - the change just is not flushed until save
Chained indexing produces a copy, so the assignment lands on a temporary

items.rationale: The mask produces a new object; assigning to it discards the result. Use `.loc[mask, 'flag'] = 1`.

items.stem: What is the effect of starting a bar chart's y-axis above zero?

options.text: It exaggerates differences, because bar length is the encoding
Nothing, as long as the axis is labelled
It compresses differences, making them harder to see
It is required whenever the values are large

items.rationale: Bars encode value as length from a baseline. Move the baseline and the lengths stop being proportional to the values.

items.stem: You need to compare one metric across 40 categories. Which chart reads most easily?

options.text: A pie chart with 40 slices
A horizontal bar chart sorted by value
A 3D column chart
A stacked area chart

items.rationale: Horizontal bars give long labels room, and sorting turns rank into position, which is the most accurately read encoding.

items.stem: A model scores 99% on training data and 62% on held-out data. What is happening?

options.text: Underfitting - the model is too simple for the data
The model is well calibrated
Overfitting - it has memorised the training set rather than generalised
The held-out set is too large

items.rationale: A large train/test gap is the definition of overfitting.

items.stem: Why fit a feature scaler inside each cross-validation fold rather than once on the full dataset?

options.text: It is significantly faster
Scaling changes the label distribution
Scalers cannot technically be reused across folds
Fitting on everything leaks information from the validation fold into training, inflating the score

items.rationale: The scaler's statistics are learned parameters. Learning them from data you then evaluate on is leakage.

items.stem: What does `typeof null` return?

options.text: "object"
"null"
"undefined"
"number"

items.rationale: A long-standing bug in the language, kept for backwards compatibility.

items.stem: You `await` inside an `array.forEach(async (x) => ...)` callback. What happens?

options.text: It behaves exactly like `for...of` with await
forEach ignores the returned promises, so the loop finishes before the work does
It is a syntax error
The callbacks run in reverse order

items.rationale: forEach discards the callback's return value. Use `for...of` to await sequentially, or `Promise.all(map(...))` to await concurrently.

items.stem: What does a TypeScript `interface` compile to in the emitted JavaScript?

options.text: A JavaScript class
A runtime validation function
Nothing - types are erased at compile time
A JSON schema object

items.rationale: Types exist only for the compiler. Data crossing a network boundary still needs runtime validation.

items.stem: How does `any` differ from `unknown`?

options.text: They are identical aliases
`any` performs a runtime cast, `unknown` does not
`unknown` makes the value read-only
`any` switches off checking for everything reached through it; `unknown` forces you to narrow before use

items.rationale: `unknown` is the safe top type: assignable from anything, assignable to nothing without a check.

items.stem: In a production build, when does a `useEffect` with an empty dependency array run?

options.text: Once, after the first render
After every render
Never - an empty array disables it
Before the first render, synchronously

items.rationale: No dependencies means nothing can change, so it runs once after mount, with its cleanup on unmount.

items.stem: Why does using the array index as a list `key` cause bugs when the list is reordered?

options.text: Numeric keys are slower to compare than strings
The key identifies a position rather than an item, so component state stays behind with the position
React throws when keys are integers
It disables reconciliation completely

items.rationale: Reconciliation matches elements by key. If the key is the index, item 0 is always 'the same' element, so its state and DOM stay put while its data changes underneath.

items.stem: What does `display: flex` on a container do?

options.text: Makes the container itself a flex item inside its own parent
Applies flex layout to every descendant at any depth
Lays out its direct children along a main axis
Acts as a shorthand for floating the children left

items.rationale: Flex layout applies to direct children only; grandchildren are laid out by their own parent's display value.

items.stem: Why prefer a `<button>` over a `<div>` with a click handler?

options.text: It renders measurably faster
A div cannot receive click events
CSS cannot style a div's hover state
It is keyboard-focusable, activates on Enter and Space, and is announced as a button by assistive tech

items.rationale: Reproducing focus, key handling and the accessibility role by hand is work the native element has already done.

items.stem: How does Node.js execute your JavaScript?

options.text: On a single thread with an event loop, with I/O handled off that thread
One operating-system thread per incoming request
One process per incoming request
Fully synchronously, in call order

items.rationale: Your code runs on one thread. Concurrency comes from not blocking it while I/O completes elsewhere.

items.stem: What does a long CPU-bound loop inside a request handler do to the server?

options.text: It is automatically moved to a worker thread
It blocks the event loop, so every other in-flight request stalls
It slows only that one request
libuv schedules it on the thread pool

items.rationale: The thread pool handles certain I/O and crypto calls, not your JavaScript. CPU-bound work belongs in a worker thread or a separate process.

items.stem: Which HTTP method is required to be idempotent?

options.text: POST
PATCH
PUT
None of them

items.rationale: PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST and PATCH are not required to be.

items.stem: You add a new required field to an existing endpoint's request body. What is the effect on existing clients?

options.text: It is backwards compatible, since their old fields still work
It is safe as long as it is documented
Only GET requests are affected
It is a breaking change - their previously valid requests now fail validation

items.rationale: Adding optional fields is compatible; making anything newly required is not.

items.stem: A test passes and fails intermittently on unchanged code. What is the real cost?

options.text: It teaches the team to ignore red builds, which hides genuine failures
Nothing, as long as it passes most of the time
It proves the code is fast enough
It correctly detects a race condition on every run

items.rationale: A flaky test destroys the signal the suite exists to provide. Fix it or delete it.

items.stem: What goes wrong if you mock the module you are trying to test?

options.text: Nothing - that is the standard unit-testing approach
The test asserts on the mock's behaviour, so the real code is never exercised
The assertions run more slowly
Async code stops working

items.rationale: Mock the collaborators at the boundary, never the subject under test.

items.stem: What does `git revert <commit>` do?

options.text: Deletes the commit from the history
Moves HEAD back one commit and discards the working tree
Creates a new commit that undoes that commit's changes, leaving history intact
Stashes the changes for later

items.rationale: revert is additive and therefore safe on shared branches; `reset` is the one that rewrites.

items.stem: What is the risk of force-pushing a rebased branch that colleagues have already pulled?

options.text: Git merges their work into the rebase automatically
Git refuses the push in all cases
Nothing - other clones are unaffected
Shared history is rewritten, so their branches diverge and their merges can resurrect old commits

items.rationale: Rebasing rewrites commit ids. Anyone who already has the old ids now has a different history from yours.

items.stem: What permissions does `chmod 640 report.csv` set?

options.text: Owner read and write, group read, others nothing
Owner read, write and execute; group read and write; others read
Owner read only, group read and write, others nothing
Everyone read and write

items.rationale: Each digit sums r=4, w=2, x=1: 6 = rw, 4 = r, 0 = none.

items.stem: In the pipeline `build | tee log.txt`, what does `tee` receive?

options.text: Both stdout and stderr
Only build's stdout - its stderr still goes to the terminal
Build's exit code
Only stderr

items.rationale: A pipe connects stdout. To include stderr you have to redirect it explicitly, e.g. `2>&1`.

items.stem: Why do Dockerfiles copy the dependency manifest and install dependencies before copying the rest of the source?

options.text: Because copying the whole source first would fail
It halves the size of the final image
So the dependency-install layer stays cached when only application code changes
Instruction order has no effect on builds

items.rationale: Each instruction is a cached layer invalidated by its inputs. Source changes far more often than dependencies.

items.stem: What happens to data an application writes into its container's own filesystem?

options.text: It is written back into the image
It survives removal of the container automatically
It is shared with every other container from the same image
It is lost when the container is removed, unless the path is a volume or bind mount

items.rationale: The writable layer belongs to the container, not the image, and dies with it. State needs a volume or an external service.

items.stem: What is a Kubernetes Deployment responsible for?

options.text: Keeping the declared number of pod replicas running and managing rollouts between versions
Giving pods a stable network address and load balancing to them
Storing non-secret configuration for pods to consume
Running a task on a cron schedule

items.rationale: Addressing is a Service, configuration is a ConfigMap, and scheduled work is a CronJob.

items.stem: A pod's readiness probe starts failing. What does Kubernetes do?

options.text: Restarts the container immediately
Removes it from Service endpoints so it stops receiving traffic, but does not restart it
Deletes the pod and schedules a replacement
Nothing - readiness probes are advisory only

items.rationale: Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts. Confusing the two is how a slow-starting service ends up in a restart loop.

items.stem: What is wrong with putting deployment credentials directly in the pipeline definition file?

options.text: Nothing, provided the repository is private
It is required for builds to be reproducible
Anyone with read access to the repository gets them, and they persist in history after removal
It is the only way a runner can authenticate

items.rationale: Secrets belong in the CI system's secret store, injected at run time. A committed secret has to be rotated, not just deleted.

items.stem: What characterises a blue/green deployment?

options.text: Half the fleet permanently runs the previous version
Instances are replaced one at a time until all are new
Releases happen only inside a maintenance window
The new version runs alongside the old, and traffic is switched over once it is healthy

items.rationale: Two complete environments and one switch, which makes rollback a switch back. Replacing instances one at a time is a rolling update.

items.stem: Under the shared responsibility model, what does the cloud provider secure?

options.text: The underlying infrastructure - your configuration, data and access control remain yours
Everything, including your access policies
Only the physical building
Only billing and metering

items.rationale: Security *of* the cloud is theirs; security *in* the cloud is yours.

items.stem: What causes most cloud data exposure incidents?

options.text: The provider's own infrastructure being breached
Over-permissive access configuration by the customer
Weaknesses in the encryption algorithms used
Physical theft of disks from data centres

items.rationale: Publicly readable buckets and over-broad roles, not provider compromise. Default-deny and least privilege are the defence.

items.stem: Why keep infrastructure state in a shared remote backend with locking?

options.text: To make plan output render faster
To encrypt the provider credentials
So two concurrent applies cannot race and corrupt the recorded state
To allow modules to be published publicly

items.rationale: State is the map from code to real resources. Two writers without a lock can lose or duplicate resources.

items.stem: Someone resolves an incident by changing a managed resource in the cloud console. What is the consequence?

options.text: The change is imported into state automatically
Nothing - the next plan will simply skip that resource
The provider blocks manual edits to managed resources
Drift - the next apply may revert or destroy the change without warning

items.rationale: Declarative tools reconcile reality to the code. Manual changes must be written back into the code, or they are temporary.

items.stem: An alert fires several times a week and is routinely dismissed without action. What should happen to it?

options.text: It should be made actionable or deleted - as it stands it trains people to ignore the pager
It should be routed to more people so someone eventually acts
It should be left alone; frequent alerts prove good coverage
Its threshold should be lowered so it fires sooner

items.rationale: Every alert should correspond to something a human must do now. Anything else erodes the response to the real ones.

items.stem: What question does distributed tracing answer that metrics and logs alone struggle with?

options.text: How much disk space remains on a node
Where a single slow request spent its time as it crossed service boundaries
How many errors occurred in total today
Which CPU model the host is running

items.rationale: Metrics aggregate away the individual request; logs are per-service. A trace stitches one request's spans back together.

items.stem: Geometrically, what does multiplying a vector by a matrix do?

options.text: Always increases the vector's length
Computes the average of its components
Applies a linear transformation - some combination of rotation, scaling, shear and projection
Sorts its components in ascending order

items.rationale: The matrix's columns say where the basis vectors land; everything else follows by linearity.

items.stem: For matrices A and B, when does AB = BA?

options.text: Always
Whenever both are square
Whenever both are invertible
Only in special cases - matrix multiplication does not commute in general

items.rationale: Composition of transformations is order-dependent: rotating then scaling is not the same as scaling then rotating.

items.stem: Why does a neural network need non-linear activation functions?

options.text: Without them any stack of layers collapses into a single linear transformation
To make training converge faster
To normalise the input features
To prevent numerical overflow

items.rationale: A composition of linear maps is linear. Depth only buys expressiveness once a non-linearity sits between the layers.

items.stem: What does dropout do?

options.text: Permanently removes neurons found to be unused
Randomly zeroes activations during training only, and is disabled at inference
Is applied at inference time to add output diversity
Drops training rows that produce a high loss

items.rationale: It stops units co-adapting during training. Forgetting to switch it off at inference is a classic source of unstable predictions.

items.stem: What causes training/serving skew?

options.text: The model was trained for too few epochs
The learning rate was too small
Features are computed differently in the training pipeline than in production
The random seed differed between runs

items.rationale: Two implementations of the same feature drift apart. Sharing one transformation path between training and serving is the fix.

items.stem: A deployed model's accuracy degrades over months with no code change. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A memory leak in the serving process
Numerical overflow accumulating in the weights
Nothing can change without a deploy
Drift - the live data distribution has moved away from the training data

items.rationale: The world changes even when the model does not, which is why production models need monitoring and retraining, not just a launch.

items.stem: Why are users assigned to A and B at random?

options.text: So the groups are comparable and any difference can be attributed to the change
So the test reaches significance sooner
To spread load evenly across servers
To guarantee both groups end up exactly the same size

items.rationale: Randomisation balances both known and unknown confounders in expectation. Nothing else in the design does that.

items.stem: You check results daily and stop as soon as p < 0.05. What does that do?

options.text: Nothing - it is the standard way to run a test
Inflates the false positive rate well above 5%
Has no effect once the sample is large
Reduces the false positive rate

items.rationale: Repeated looks give the noise repeated chances to cross the line. Fix the sample size in advance, or use a sequential test designed for peeking.

items.stem: After `a = [1, 2, 3]`, `b = a`, `b.append(4)` — what is `a`?

options.text: It raises a TypeError

items.rationale: Assignment binds a second name to the same list object; it does not copy it.

items.stem: A loop does `for i in range(3): funcs.append(lambda: i)`. Every function returns 2. Why?

options.text: range() is evaluated lazily, so only the last value survives
The lambda closes over the variable `i`, which is 2 once the loop ends
Lambdas cannot capture loop variables at all
All three lambdas are actually the same object

items.rationale: Closures capture the variable, not its value at the moment they are created. A default argument freezes the value instead.

items.stem: Does `WHERE col <> "x"` return the rows where `col` is NULL?

options.text: Yes, since NULL is not equal to that value
Only if the column is indexed
No — a comparison with NULL is unknown, so those rows are excluded
No, and the query raises an error

items.rationale: NULL comparisons evaluate to unknown rather than true, so the filter drops them. Add an explicit IS NULL test if you want them back.

items.stem: How does `COUNT(col)` differ from `COUNT(*)`?

options.text: They are always identical
`COUNT(col)` is faster but approximate
`COUNT(*)` is the one that skips NULLs
It skips rows where `col` is NULL

items.rationale: `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` counts non-null values of that column.

items.stem: Ice cream sales and drownings correlate at 0.9. What follows?

options.text: Nothing causal — a common cause, such as hot weather, can produce this
Ice cream consumption causes drownings
The correlation must be a calculation error
At least one of the variables is normally distributed

items.rationale: A confounder influencing both variables produces correlation with no causal link between them.

items.stem: You run 20 independent tests at alpha = 0.05 on data with no real effect. How many significant results should you expect?

options.text: None, because there is no real effect
About 1
About 5
About 10

items.rationale: Each test carries a 5% false positive rate, so 20 x 0.05 = 1. This is why multiple comparisons need a correction.

items.stem: 99% of your rows are class A. A model that always predicts A scores 99% accuracy. What does that tell you?

options.text: The model has learned the task well
The dataset needs more features
Accuracy is uninformative here — precision, recall or a balanced metric is needed
The model is overfitting

items.rationale: On imbalanced data the majority-class baseline already scores high, so accuracy cannot separate a good model from a useless one.

items.stem: Why keep a test set separate from the validation set used for tuning?

options.text: To double the amount of training data
Because validation sets are always too small to trust
To make training run faster
Tuning against validation makes that score optimistic, so an untouched set is needed for an honest estimate

items.rationale: Every tuning decision leaks a little validation information into the model. Only data never used for any decision gives an unbiased estimate.

items.stem: Why is dropping every row with a missing value risky?

options.text: Missingness is often not random, so the rows that survive are a biased sample
It always leaves too few rows to model
It silently changes the column data types
Most tools forbid it

items.rationale: If values go missing for a reason related to the outcome, dropping those rows removes exactly the cases you needed.

items.stem: A date column read as text sorts "2024-10-01" before "2024-9-01". Why?

options.text: The two dates are in different time zones
It is being sorted as text, where "1" comes before "9"
October genuinely precedes September in ISO ordering
The sort defaulted to descending

items.rationale: Text sorts character by character. Parsing to a real date type, or zero-padding the month, fixes the order.

items.stem: Why are rainbow colour maps discouraged for continuous data?

options.text: They render more slowly than other maps
They cannot represent negative values
They are not perceptually uniform, so they create banding the data does not contain
They require a legend, unlike other maps

items.rationale: Equal steps in the data become unequal steps in perceived colour, inventing boundaries where the data is smooth.

items.stem: When is a chart with two different y-axes misleading?

options.text: Only when the two series use different units
Only when there are more than two series
Never, as long as both axes are labelled
Almost always — the two scales can be chosen to manufacture or hide a relationship

items.rationale: The apparent crossing point is an artefact of two independently chosen scales. Small multiples, or indexing both series to a common baseline, are honest alternatives.

items.stem: Why version the training data alongside the model?

options.text: Without it you cannot reproduce a result or explain a regression
To reduce storage costs
Because models cannot load unversioned data
To make training run faster

items.rationale: A model is a function of its code and its data. Versioning only the code leaves half the experiment unrecorded.

items.stem: What is a shadow deployment?

options.text: The model runs only outside business hours
The new model scores live traffic in parallel, but its predictions are not served to users
A standby copy runs on a second server purely for failover
Traffic is split evenly between the old and new versions

items.rationale: It measures the new model on real traffic with no user-facing risk. Splitting traffic between versions is an A/B test, not a shadow.

items.stem: What does a learning rate that is far too large usually cause?

options.text: Slow but steady convergence
Overfitting to the training set
The loss to oscillate or diverge instead of converging
Vanishing gradients

items.rationale: Each step overshoots the minimum, so the loss bounces around or grows rather than settling.

items.stem: Why does batch normalisation behave differently at inference?

options.text: It is switched off entirely
It normalises across features rather than across examples
It is replaced by layer normalisation
It uses running statistics collected during training instead of the current batch

items.rationale: Inference may see a single example, where batch statistics are meaningless, so stored population estimates are used instead.
